title: Proposal: %T Prompt parameter for psql for current time (like Oracle has)

decisive_objections.quote: I'm not really convinced that %`date` isn't a usable solution for this, especially since it seems like a very niche requirement. The next person who wants it might well have a different desire than you for exactly what gets shown. The output of date can be customized, but a hard-wired prompt.c feature not so much.
On the whole I'd rather not eat more of the limited namespace for psql prompt codes for this.

I'm not sure if the *prompt* is a sensible place for it though. The place it seems like it would be most useful is reading the output of script executions where there would be no prompts. Perhaps it's the command tags and \echo statements that should be timestamped.

outcome_summary: Kirk proposed a fixed %T prompt escape printing the client's current time as HH24:MI:SS (explicitly no date, no format options). Tom Lane objected immediately that %`date` already covers it, that one hard-wired format won't fit the next user, and that prompt-escape namespace is scarce; in April Greg Stark and Tom Lane added that one timestamp format can't satisfy everyone and that timestamps belong on command tags / \echo output rather than the prompt. CF 4227 (v2/v3 patch) was closed Returned with feedback in CF 2023-07 (Daniel Gustafsson: it had not built since the March CF) and was never resubmitted.
notes: Shape differs slightly from the brief: Kirk's version is %T = current client time HH24:MI:SS in the psql PROMPT only; he explicitly rejected adding the date. Command-output timestamps were Greg Stark's counter-suggestion (2023-04-09), not Kirk's proposal. Formal CF status is 'Returned with feedback' (closing reason given: patch did not build), not 'Rejected'; the substantive objections are Tom's and Greg's. The same thread also spawned Kirk's companion proposal ':SQL_EXEC_TIME (like :ROW_COUNT)' (2023-02-23, subject change mid-thread). CUTOFF CAVEAT: Tom's objection came 38 minutes after the proposal on the same day (archive shows 17:17:46 vs 17:55:25), so with day granularity cutoff_date equals first_message_date: the tool must be given the first message itself plus nothing else; a timestamp cutoff of 2023-02-22T17:55 (archive time) would be precise. Nikolay Samokhvalov (the user) replied in-thread and is listed as a CF reviewer. Blind: message 2 is Nikolay Samokhvalov's supportive reply; Tom Lane's objection is message 3, so blind_n=2.

title: PoC: pg_dump --filter-data <file> (like Oracle Where Clause on RMAN for specific tables)

decisive_objections.quote: Have you considered partitioning these tables by date and then not dumping the older partitions? That would fit into existing functionality a lot better.
Rather than invent new flags, I think a better approach would be to convince pg_dump to dump a view, such that table foo has a view fooslice to limit / filter the output.

While we could make the view mapping into a separate filtering file as you suggest, that's more complexity and also a little more dangerous in an action-at-a-distance way, so I'd rather have people be very specific in the mapping on the command line.

title: Support for unsigned integer types

decisive_objections.quote: This has been discussed before, and we've concluded that the impact on the numeric promotion hierarchy (that is, implicit-cast rules among the integer types) would probably be catastrophic, leading to problems like ambiguous-operator errors in many cases that were fine before. Quick, is "42 + 1" an int32 or uint32 operation?
Plus, the sheer magnitude of effort needed to build out a reasonable set of support (functions, operators, opclasses) for uint types seems daunting.
Here is an extension that implements this: https://github.com/petere/pguint

earlier_attempts.summary: 'Is there any plan to add unsigned integer types?' (question, no patch); answered with existing alternatives

outcome_summary: A user asked for uint32/uint64 in core. Tom Lane answered that adding them to the implicit-cast promotion hierarchy would cause widespread ambiguous-operator breakage, while keeping them outside it would make them unusable, and that the support surface (functions, operators, opclasses) is daunting; Peter Eisentraut pointed to his pguint extension. No patch followed.
notes: This is a feature request without a patch, so 'rejected' = turned down on the list. Category for the cast-hierarchy objection is approximate (it is really type-system / implicit-cast semantics; the closest listed category is 'SQL standard/syntax'). The 2011 thread is one earlier instance found; Tom says 'discussed before', there are likely more (not exhaustively searched; archive full-text search only covers recent mail). Blind: Tom Lane's objection is the very first reply (position 2), so blind_n=1 (proposal only). The proposal is a short feature request without a patch.

title: [PATCH] Proposal for HIDDEN/INVISIBLE column

decisive_objections.quote: So I can't see any real benefits of adding this feature to PostgreSQL. It will only make the existing code and the existing user interface even more complicated than they are now.

As for the proposal itself, I'm kind of allergic to the terminology you've suggested, because the column is in no way hidden. It's still visible in the catalogs, you can still select it explicitly, etc. Anybody who thinks this is useful from a security standpoint is mistaken, but these words suggest that it is.
BTW, you do NOT get to add an information_schema column for this. The information_schema is defined in the SQL standard.
So the more I think about this, the squishier it gets. I'm now sharing the fears expressed upthread about whether it's even possible to define this in a way that won't have a lot of gotchas.

title: Allow DELETE to use ORDER BY and LIMIT/OFFSET

decisive_objections.quote: Indeed, this is technically possible, but we've rejected the idea before and I'm not aware of any reason to change our minds.

The problem is that a partial DELETE is not very deterministic about which rows are deleted, and that does not seem like a great property for a data-updating command. (The same applies to UPDATE, which is why we don't allow these options in that command either.)
We live with this amount of indeterminism in SELECT, but that doesn't make it a brilliant idea to allow it in UPDATE/DELETE.

Daniel Loureiro: DELETE with LIMIT (or my first hack)

Surafel Temesgen: DELETE and UPDATE with LIMIT and ORDER BY

Greg Stark and Corey Huinker argued for it, but nothing was committed.

title: Patch: Global Unique Index

decisive_objections.quote: I'm not convinced that we want this feature at all: as far as I can see, it will completely destroy the benefits of making a partitioned table in the first place.
I still think this is a dead end that will never get committed.

The thing that feels insoluble is that you can't do this without acquiring sufficient locks to prevent addition of new partitions while the insertion is in progress. That will be expensive in itself, and it will turn ATTACH PARTITION into a performance disaster.

outcome_summary: Cary Huang posted a patch enforcing uniqueness across all partitions by checking every partition's local index on insert. Tom Lane argued it defeats the purpose of partitioning, would deadlock or serialize concurrent inserts across partitions, and needs locks that make ATTACH PARTITION a performance disaster; Bruce Momjian questioned how concurrent duplicate insertion is prevented. The thread petered out in 2023 and nothing was committed.
notes: cf_url null: a CF entry may exist but could not be located without login (WebSearch found none). title: Enable data checksums by default

decisive_objections.quote: My understanding was that the reason for some hesitation about adopting data checksums was the performance impact. Not the checksumming itself, but the overhead from hint bit logging. The last time I looked into that, you could get performance impacts on the order of 5% tps.
For those uses, this change would render pg_upgrade useless for upgrades from an old instance with default settings to a new instance with default settings.

earlier_attempts.summary: Christoph Berg: Enable data checksums by default; Tom Lane: 'the main value of checksums is that they allow the Postgres project to deflect blame' and asked for proof the CPU cost is justified

outcome_summary: Greg Sabino Mullane proposed flipping initdb's default to data checksums on. Peter Eisentraut raised the hint-bit WAL-logging overhead (~5% tps) and the pg_upgrade problem (old default clusters without checksums can't be upgraded into new default clusters); these were addressed by first adding initdb --no-data-checksums (983a588e0b8, 2024-10-01) and documentation, and the default was switched in PG18 (04bec894a04, 2024-10-16). The 2019 attempt had failed on Tom Lane's skepticism about the CPU cost vs. benefit.
notes: Good case for 'a naive rejector would cite performance and pg_upgrade'. cutoff_date 2024-08-08 keeps messages 1-3 (2024-08-06/07) and excludes Peter Eisentraut's objection. pg_upgrade handling remained a follow-up topic (CF 5206 'pg_upgrade: Support for upgrading to checksums enabled', not verified here). title: Add SPLIT PARTITION/MERGE PARTITIONS commands

decisive_objections.quote: This breaks from the CVE-2014-0062 (commit 5f17304) principle of not repeating name lookups. The attached demo uses this defect to make one partition have two parents.
Unfortunately, I think there are too many problems here to be reasonably fixed before release, and I think all of SPLIT/MERGE PARTITION needs to be reverted.

In both cases, we do a reverse lookup on an OID to get a name which the CREATE TABLE code will later turn back into an OID. If we don't get the same value, that's at least a bug and probably a security vulnerability, and there is no way to be certain that we will get the same value.

outcome_summary: ALTER TABLE ... MERGE PARTITIONS / SPLIT PARTITION were committed for PG17 on 2024-04-07 (1adf16b8fba, 87c21bb9412). In August 2024 Noah Misch showed the implementation repeated name lookups (CVE-2014-0062 class), and Robert Haas found more such lookups and argued that building the new partition via a synthesized CREATE TABLE through ProcessUtility was the wrong design; Korotkov reverted the whole feature before RC (3890d90c150, 2024-08-24, backpatched to 17). A reworked version was committed for PG19 on 2025-12-14 (f2e4cc42795, 4b3d173629f).
notes: commit field holds the MERGE PARTITIONS commit; SPLIT is 87c21bb9412 (same day). Revert commit message cites 'security issues related to repeatable name lookups (CVE-2014-0062)'. cutoff_date = first commit date, so the tool sees ~2 years of pre-commit review but no post-commit issue reports. Note Robert Haas also posted a design objection on 2024-04-12 (CA+TgmoYcjL+w2BQzku5iNXKR5fyxJMSP3avQta8xngioTX7D7A@mail.gmail.com: the syntax names new tables but gives no way to set their properties), after the commit. title: SQL:2011 application time (temporal PRIMARY KEY / UNIQUE / FOREIGN KEY WITHOUT OVERLAPS)

decisive_objections.quote: It looks like we missed some of these fundamental design questions early on, and it might be too late now to fix them for PG17.

I'm also concerned that if ranges have this fundamental incompatibility with periods, then the plan to eventually evolve this patch set to support standard periods will also have as-yet-unknown problems.
I'm afraid that these issues cannot be resolved in good time for this release, so we should revert this patch set for now.

outcome_summary: Temporal PRIMARY KEY/UNIQUE (46a0cd4cefb, 2024-01-24) and FOREIGN KEY (34768ee3616, 2024-03-24) constraints using WITHOUT OVERLAPS on range columns were committed for PG17. Post-commit, the author found empty ranges bypass the exclusion semantics; Peter Eisentraut judged these fundamental design questions (empty ranges, relation to SQL-standard PERIODs, implicit CHECK constraints tied to PKs) unresolvable before release and reverted the set (8aee330af55, 2024-05-16). It was re-committed for PG18 (fc0438b4e80, 2024-09-17).

The empty-range problem was raised by the author himself (Paul Jungwirth, 2024-04-03, 47550967-260b-4180-9791-b224859fe63e@illuminatedcomputing.com); Robert Haas pushed it onto the PG17 open items (2024-04-26). decisive_objections.quote: I don't think it's sane from a performance view to start a subtransaction for every coercion, particularly because most coercion paths will never trigger an error, leaving things like out-of-memory or interrupts aside.

The problem here is that this was going to be a headline new feature for v15. Shipping what apparently is only an alpha-quality implementation seems pretty problematic unless we advertise it as such, and that's not something we've done very much in the past.
It feels blatantly obvious that this code isn't even remotely close to being releasable.

title: [PATCH] GROUP BY ALL

decisive_objections.source: commit message of a32733d8f10 (local git, verified)
decisive_objections.quote: A postcommit review discovered that GROUP BY ALL missed our special handling of entries that also appear in an ORDER BY in the query. This caused the query to return wrong results when ORDER BY specifies non-default equality semantics. While this should be fixable with some refactoring, doing it cleanly seems like too much code churn for late beta. We'll revert and try again in v20.
I don't have a lot of faith that there aren't other comparable bugs lurking.
That is a large change to take on post-beta2, though. Maybe the path of prudence is to revert GROUP BY ALL for v19 and try again for v20.

In June 2026 Chao Li found that the ALL path skipped transformGroupClauseExpr()'s copying of ORDER BY operator semantics, giving wrong results with non-default equality operators (e.g. record_image_ops); Tom judged the clause-handling code too baroque to fix safely post-beta2 and it was reverted from 19 and master (a32733d8f10, 2026-07-17), to retry in v20.

title: Non-text mode for pg_dumpall (custom/directory/tar output for pg_dumpall, pg_restore support)
proposer: Andrew Dunstan (design); Mahendra Singh Thalor (patch author)

decisive_objections.quote: This uses pgdumpopts for plain mode only, so many pg_dumpall options silently have no effect in non-plain mode.

There should be one appendPQExpBuffer(delQry, "DROP ROLE ..."), not one for plain format and another for non-plain formats. Having two creates excess risk of format-specific bugs, something pg_dump.c has long avoided well.

None of this is meant to say the feature is impossible. But I don’t think this commit is at the point where post-commit fixups are the right workflow. I recommend reverting, posting a new version, and letting commitfest review finish.

title: support fast default for domain with constraints

decisive_objections.quote: This patch appears to summarily throw away a couple of backwards-compatibility concerns that the previous round took care to preserve: * not throwing an error if the default would fail the domain constraints, but the table is empty so there is no need to instantiate the default.

The fundamental problem with this whole mess is that it treats certain kinds of default-expression evaluation error (i.e., domain CHECK failures) differently from others. There is no way that that leads to a consistent user experience.

decisive_objections.source: commit message of a0354e29c41 (local git, verified)

title: sequencesync worker race with REFRESH SEQUENCES (fix: reject REFRESH SEQUENCES while a sequencesync worker runs)

decisive_objections.quote: Well, that would fix this test, but I wonder if this result isn't telling us that f38afa4ab has created a failure condition that will bite real users. Why would the user issuing REFRESH SEQUENCES be aware of whether there's a sync worker running right then? Why should it be his problem to avoid that?
I grow even more skeptical that f38afa4ab was a good idea. It seems inevitable that it will cause annoying failures in the field.

decisive_objections.source: commit message of dde9a87d4d0 (local git, verified)
decisive_objections.quote: While discussing how to fix the tests, we concluded that blocking the command while a sequencesync worker is running is inconvenient for users. So we will fix the original race differently in a follow-up commit.

outcome_summary: Noah Misch reported (from an AI-assisted review) that ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... REFRESH SEQUENCES could race with a running sequencesync worker and leave stale sequence values marked READY. Among the options discussed, the chosen fix made REFRESH SEQUENCES raise an ERROR while a sequencesync worker was running (f38afa4abb0, 2026-07-15). The buildfarm (skink under valgrind) immediately hit the new error; Tom Lane argued this was a user-facing failure mode rather than a test problem, and Amit Kapila reverted it (dde9a87d4d0, 2026-07-18) to fix the race another way.
